questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When a charged particle at rest experiences zero electromagnetic force,
options: the electric field must be zero
the magnetic field must be zero
the electric field might or might not be zero
the magnetic field might or might not be zero
questions.solution:
The electromagnetic force on a charged particle is given by the Lorentz force equation:

$\vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v} \times \vec{B})$

Since the particle is at rest, its velocity $\vec{v} = 0$. The magnetic force component is $q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B}) = 0$, irrespective of the magnetic field $\vec{B}$.

The total force reduces to $\vec{F} = q\vec{E}$.

Given that the total electromagnetic force is zero, we have $q\vec{E} = 0$. Since the particle is charged ($q \neq 0$), the electric field $\vec{E}$ must be zero.

The magnetic field $\vec{B}$ does not exert any force on a particle at rest, so it might or might not be zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Suppose a charged particle is projected inside a gravity-free room and experiences a deflection. Which of the following statements apply?
options: the two fields cannot both be zero
a magnetic field is necessarily present
an electric field is necessarily present
the two fields can both be nonzero
questions.solution:
The force on a moving charge $q$ with velocity $\vec{v}$ in an electric field $\vec{E}$ and magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is given by the Lorentz force:

$\vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v} \times \vec{B})$

For the particle to experience a deflection, the net force perpendicular to its velocity must be non-zero.

If both $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{B}$ are zero, the net force is zero, and the particle will move in a straight line without any deflection. Hence, the two fields cannot both be zero.

A deflection can be caused by an electric field alone (if $\vec{E}$ has a component perpendicular to $\vec{v}$) or by a magnetic field alone (if $\vec{B}$ has a component perpendicular to $\vec{v}$). Thus, neither a magnetic field nor an electric field is necessarily present.

Both fields can also be non-zero simultaneously and produce a net force that causes deflection.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When a charged particle held at rest experiences an electromagnetic force,
options: the electric field cannot be zero
the magnetic field might or might not be zero
the electric field might or might not be zero
the magnetic field cannot be zero
questions.solution:
The electromagnetic force on a charged particle is given by the Lorentz force equation:

$\vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v} \times \vec{B})$

Since the charged particle is at rest, its velocity $\vec{v} = 0$. Substituting this into the force equation gives:

$\vec{F} = q\vec{E}$

It is given that the particle experiences an electromagnetic force, so $\vec{F} \neq 0$. This implies that $q\vec{E} \neq 0$, and hence the electric field $\vec{E}$ cannot be zero.

The magnetic force term $q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$ is zero regardless of the value of the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ because $\vec{v} = 0$. Thus, the magnetic field might or might not be zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charged particle travels along a circle under the influence of possible constant electric and magnetic fields. Which of the following conditions is possible?
questions.solution:
For a charged particle to move in a circle, its speed must remain constant. This implies that the net work done by the fields on the particle must be zero at all times.

The magnetic force $\vec{F}_m = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$ is always perpendicular to the velocity $\vec{v}$, so it does no work.

The power delivered by the electric field is $P = q\vec{E} \cdot \vec{v}$. For the speed to be constant, we must have $q\vec{E} \cdot \vec{v} = 0$ at all times. Since the particle is moving in a circle, its velocity vector continuously changes direction in the plane of the circle. For the dot product to be zero at all points on the circle, the electric field $\vec{E}$ must be perpendicular to the plane of the circle.

If $\vec{E}$ is perpendicular to the plane of the circle, it will exert a constant force $q\vec{E}$ perpendicular to the plane. To keep the particle in the circular plane, the net force in the perpendicular direction must be zero. The magnetic force perpendicular to the plane is given by the component of $q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$ along $\vec{E}$. Since $\vec{v}$ continuously changes direction, this component of the magnetic force will vary sinusoidally and cannot cancel the constant electric force $q\vec{E}$.

Therefore, the electric field must be zero ($E = 0$).

To provide the necessary centripetal force for circular motion, a magnetic field must be present. Thus, $B \neq 0$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charged particle travels undeflected through a region containing an electric and a magnetic field. It is possible that
questions.solution:
The Lorentz force on a charged particle is given by $\vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v} \times \vec{B})$.

For the particle to travel undeflected, the net force must either be zero or parallel to its velocity $\vec{v}$.

If $\vec{F} = 0$, then $\vec{E} = -(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$. This implies $\vec{E}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{B}$. Thus, $\vec{E}$ is not parallel to $\vec{B}$, making option (1) possible.

If $\vec{E} \parallel \vec{B}$ and $\vec{v} \parallel \vec{E}$, then $\vec{v} \parallel \vec{B}$, which gives $\vec{v} \times \vec{B} = 0$. The net force is $\vec{F} = q\vec{E}$. Since $\vec{E} \parallel \vec{v}$, the force is parallel to the velocity. The particle accelerates or decelerates along a straight line without deflection, making option (3) possible.

For option (2), if $\vec{v} \parallel \vec{B}$, the magnetic force is zero. For no deflection, the electric force $q\vec{E}$ must be parallel to $\vec{v}$, meaning $\vec{E} \parallel \vec{v} \parallel \vec{B}$. This contradicts the given condition that $\vec{E}$ is not parallel to $\vec{B}$.

For option (4), if $\vec{E} \parallel \vec{B}$ and $\vec{v}$ is not parallel to $\vec{E}$, the magnetic force is non-zero and perpendicular to $\vec{B}$, while the electric force is parallel to $\vec{B}$. The net force cannot be parallel to $\vec{v}$, causing the particle to deflect.

Answer: $\vec{E}$ is not parallel to $\vec{B}$; $\vec{E} \parallel \vec{B}$, $\vec{v} \parallel \vec{E}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charged particle travels in a gravity-free space without any change in velocity. Which of the following could be possible?
questions.solution:
The net force on a charged particle in an electric and magnetic field is given by the Lorentz force:

$\vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v} imes \vec{B})$

For the particle to travel without any change in velocity, the net force must be zero, i.e., $\vec{F} = 0$.

If $E = 0$ and $B = 0$, then $\vec{F} = 0$. This is possible.

If $E = 0$ and $B eq 0$, then $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} imes \vec{B})$. If the particle moves parallel or anti-parallel to the magnetic field ($\vec{v} \parallel \vec{B}$), then $\vec{v} imes \vec{B} = 0$ and $\vec{F} = 0$. This is possible.

If $E eq 0$ and $B eq 0$, then $\vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v} imes \vec{B})$. If $\vec{E} = -(\vec{v} imes \vec{B})$, which happens when $\vec{E}$, $\vec{v}$, and $\vec{B}$ are mutually perpendicular and $E = vB$, then $\vec{F} = 0$. This is possible.

If $E eq 0$ and $B = 0$, then $\vec{F} = q\vec{E} eq 0$. The particle will accelerate, and its velocity will change. This is not possible.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electron travels along the positive $x$-axis. A magnetic field is to be applied for a brief duration to reverse the electron's direction, making it move parallel to the negative $x$-axis. This can be achieved by directing the magnetic field along the
questions.solution:
The initial velocity of the electron is $\vec{v} = v\hat{i}$.

To reverse the direction of the electron such that it moves parallel to the negative $x$-axis, it must complete a semi-circular path. This requires a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the initial velocity.

Since the initial velocity is along the $x$-axis, the magnetic field must lie in the $y$-$z$ plane.

If the magnetic field is directed along the $y$-axis ($\vec{B} = B\hat{j}$), the magnetic force is $\vec{F} = -e(v\hat{i} \times B\hat{j}) = -evB\hat{k}$. The electron moves in a semi-circle in the $x$-$z$ plane, and its direction is reversed.

If the magnetic field is directed along the $z$-axis ($\vec{B} = B\hat{k}$), the magnetic force is $\vec{F} = -e(v\hat{i} \times B\hat{k}) = evB\hat{j}$. The electron moves in a semi-circle in the $x$-$y$ plane, and its direction is reversed.

Thus, the magnetic field can be along the $y$-axis or the $z$-axis. The options stating "only" are incorrect.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If a charged particle travels without acceleration in a region containing electric and magnetic fields,
questions.solution:
The Lorentz force on a charged particle is given by $\vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v} \times \vec{B})$.

For the particle to move without acceleration, the net force must be zero:

$q(\vec{E} + \vec{v} \times \vec{B}) = 0$

$\vec{E} = -(\vec{v} \times \vec{B}) = \vec{B} \times \vec{v}$

From the properties of the cross product, the vector $\vec{E}$ must be perpendicular to both $\vec{B}$ and $\vec{v}$.

Therefore, $\vec{E} \perp \vec{B}$ and $\vec{v} \perp \vec{E}$.

The magnitude of the electric field is $E = vB \sin \theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{B}$. Thus, $E$ is not necessarily equal to $vB$, and $\vec{v}$ is not necessarily perpendicular to $\vec{B}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider two ions of equal mass, where one is singly-ionized while the other is doubly-ionized. They are projected from an identical location into a uniform magnetic field, sharing the same initial velocity perpendicular to the field.
options: Both ions will follow circles of equal radii.
The circle described by the singly-ionized ion will have a radius twice that of the other circle.
The two circles touch one another.
The two circles do not touch one another.
questions.solution:
The radius of the circular path of a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field is given by $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$.

For the singly-ionized ion, the charge is $q_1 = e$, so its radius is $r_1 = \dfrac{mv}{eB}$.

For the doubly-ionized ion, the charge is $q_2 = 2e$, so its radius is $r_2 = \dfrac{mv}{2eB}$.

Comparing the two radii, we get $r_1 = 2r_2$. Thus, the circle described by the singly-ionized ion has a radius twice that of the doubly-ionized ion.

Since both ions are projected from the same location with the same initial velocity, their circular paths share a common tangent at the point of projection. Because they are tangent to the same line at the same point, the two circles touch each other at this initial point.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Suppose $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{B}$ represent the electric and magnetic fields in a reference frame $S$, while $\vec{E}'$ and $\vec{B}'$ represent them in another frame $S'$ that moves with a velocity $\vec{v}$ relative to $S$. Which two of the following equations are incorrect?
questions.solution:
The Lorentz transformations for the transverse components of electric and magnetic fields in SI units, for a frame $S'$ moving with velocity $v$ along the x-axis relative to $S$, are given by:

$E_y' = \gamma (E_y - v B_z)$

$B_y' = \gamma \left(B_y + $\dfrac{v}{c^2}$E_z\right)$

where $\gamma = $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}.

For non-relativistic speeds ($v \ll c$), $\gamma \approx 1$, and the equations approximate to:

$E_y' \approx E_y - v B_z$

$B_y' \approx B_y + $\dfrac{v}{c^2}$E_z$

This can also be verified using dimensional analysis. In SI units, the dimensions of electric field $E$ and magnetic field $B$ are related by $[E] = [vB]$.

Thus, the term $v B_z$ has the dimensions of an electric field, making equation (1) dimensionally correct.

Similarly, the term \dfrac{v E_z}{c^2} has the dimensions of \dfrac{[v][vB]}{[v^2]} = [$B]$, making equation (4) dimensionally correct.

Equations (2) and (3) are dimensionally inconsistent because \dfrac{v B_z}{c^2} does not have the dimensions of an electric field, and $v E_z does not have the dimensions of a magnetic field.

Therefore, equations (2) and (3) are incorrect.$
